utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting -- well, first of all, Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I'd like to address the Defence in relation to the reopening of the Prosecution's case in chief. On the 23rd of October, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's motion to reopen its case to present the evidence of 13 witnesses. Three of these 13 witnesses already appeared during the Prosecution's case as expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As such, the Chamber understands the Prosecution to seek their recall to present further evidence. As the Chamber still has to decide whether the disclosed reports fall into the expertise of these experts, the Chamber instructs the Defence to include its position on the procedural question of recalling the witnesses in its Rule 94 bis notice. Good morning, Mr. Kralj. Mr. Kralj, before we continue I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. McCloskey will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go back to the intercept that we left off, it was 65 ter 25113.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, as you'll recall, I believe you agreed with me that this was an intercept where Mr. Obucina was calling and co-ordinating with General Tolimir about issues related to approvals for Srebrenica. And just taking a look at that, do you still agree that that -- that's fundamentally what this is about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if I could, I want to ask you about one comment that the General Tolimir makes, it's near the bottom of the page. It's the box where we see three lines of his speaking. And Tolimir says: "The commander gave him approval for what he requested. Milos failed to understand and the commander approved what can go in and out of Srebrenica." Now can you tell us who General Tolimir, in your view, is referring to when he says "the commander"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the commander would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you gave the same answer to Madam Fauveau in 2008, did you not? In your answer, you said: "Always Mladic. General Mladic." Does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the term "commander in the Main Staff" is mentioned, then it would be General Mladic, and yes, it does sound familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 25113 will be Exhibit P6857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6857 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now you also talked about the topic of the final clearance for a convoy into the Republika Srpska, and would you agree with me that that was always given by the Main Staff? They were always the ones that, for security reasons and others, determined the security route and gave the final clearance for a convoy to enter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if General Mladic did not want a particular humanitarian or UNPROFOR convoy to go into the RS, he could prevent that from happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not very clear when you say if he wanted or didn't want a convoy to go through. If there was a reason, a convoy would not be allowed to go through and it really did not depend on what Mladic wanted or didn't want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could General Mladic order a convoy not to go through?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General could give that order but if there was a reason behind that, a justified reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, General Mladic controlled what went in and out of the Republika Srpska, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally he did have an insight into those things, but that was not his only task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that. Let's go on to another subject. You talked a lot about what you had learned about what was going on in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to 65 ter 04819.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, I -- this is a photograph that was taken by a Dutch soldier, a lieutenant named Johannes Rutten who testified in April 2000 in the Krstic case that this was a photograph he took during his time at Srebrenica, which was from January 1995 to July 1995. He explained that this was the UNPROFOR garbage truck dumping their garbage on a hill-side and this was the population -- some of the population of Srebrenica foraging [Realtime transcript read in error "forging"] for food in their garbage. Did you know that in the winter of 1995 this is what the population of -- some of the population of Srebrenica was doing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen this photo before. I'm not familiar with this. It may have been edited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't -- you don't know -- you didn't have any information that the population was starving during the winter of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you are recorded as having said "forging for food" when you talked about this part of the population that was at the dump. The transcript says you said "forging." I don't think you said "forging."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can simplify it by saying "looking" for food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would have meant another word and I -- but all right. I would offer this into evidence and I can offer the four pages of Rutten's testimony that would authenticate it given the challenge of the witness. And Rutten's four pages are 65 ter 31494, pages 1 through 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object to introducing the statement of the witness in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And reasons for your objections are?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the witness should be here and testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would agree had it been a full statement, 92 bis or -- would apply. But this is four pages where he merely authenticates that he took this photograph, gives us the time-frame, and what he believes is happening in it. Perhaps Mr. Lukic would agree with my summary of what he said. I'm fine with either. But I think given that what the witness has said, that it would be helpful and important for the Court to have this factual information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, does Rule 92 bis not apply if you have a short statement or just a couple of -- a short testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't -- I think the Court has quite a bit of discretion in this area and that if it is something that is simple and direct as something as a -- the authentication of a photograph, that you have the discretion, I think under 89(C), to make an exception. And I don't think 92 bis is all-encompassing to something this brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any further submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can assist the Court by briefly noting a couple of the comments that Lieutenant Rutten makes so you can see what we're talking about specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the issue is we're hearing at this moment the evidence of this witness. The witness says that he doesn't know anything about it, so that's through the back door now the -- we start with the paragraph, the photograph which in itself which shows a kind of two vehicles, one picture taken from one vehicle, a large group of people elsewhere, and you interpret what it is. And then the witness says, "I do not know anything about it." And now to -- the issue is -- Mr. Lukic, apart from that this witness doesn't know anything about it, is there any disagreement on what this picture purports to present?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I have made connection between the picture and his testimony, so I'm just reading the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you would do that, we will have it marked for identification, the photograph, for the time being, and we'll consider your -- your tendering of a portion of the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Rutten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could, as I know you have explained many times, that -- that even if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should speak not at the volume audible for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It -- that even if a witness doesn't know anything about a particular document, if they are speaking to the subject of the document, and of course this witness has spoken to restrictions and the condition of the Muslims at length --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- in his statement and in his testimony, and of course this document goes to the heart of that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter. Madam Registrar, could you please assign numbers first of all to the photograph and second to the excerpt of the testimony of Mr. Rutten.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the photograph having 65 ter 04819 will be assigned number P6858. And the four-page statement having 65 ter number 31494 will receive number P6859.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to call your attention to a statement made from a tape that this Trial Chamber has heard where Colonel Obradovic identified the voice on the tape as General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this was in P1789.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the statement says: "How many humanitarian aid convoys will," and then it's incomprehensible, "about which they argued with me for a year and until I took everything did not let anything through. I would not have taken Srebrenica or Zepa if I had not starved them in the winter. Since February, I let through only one or two convoys." This was Mladic's attitude towards the enclaves, wasn't it? From your work with him.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of this statement. I am not familiar with a position of his towards convoys. I only know what was noted on the approvals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 31500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's on the same subject. I'm showing you an outgoing code cable to Annan from -- in the United Nations New York from Akashi. And I want to take you to the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be probably page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And here it says: "None of the UNHCR convoys to the enclaves have received clearance. The Srebrenica convoy has been cancelled. The Sarajevo convoy has not left Zenica. The BSA," meaning Bosnian Serb army, "are demanding a 50-50 share of the aid to which UNHCR will not agree. The UNPF resupply convoys have suffered a similar fate. The two convoys to Gorazde were blocked by the BSA and have returned to Sarajevo. The convoy scheduled to depart from Zagreb for Sarajevo has not yet received clearance." And we can see a date of 14 June 1995. So this demand for a 50-50 share was -- of the convoys would have been something you must have known about in your work. Where was this coming from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state co-ordination humanitarian body was in charge of the distribution policy. Therefore, I'm not familiar with this, and I'm also not familiar with the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31500 will be Exhibit P6860.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6860 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go now to 65 ter 17806.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, as we're waiting, this is another outgoing code cable to Annan from Akashi. Akashi is in Zagreb by the way. This one is now dated 6 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page -- well, let's see that first page just to -- so we can orient ourselves to the people and the dates. We see its subject is entitled: "Humanitarian Situation in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now let's go to page 2 for the English under paragraph 4. And it should be page 2 to 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Take a bit of time to read it. And we can see under the eastern enclaves that it says: "UNHCR aid deliveries to the eastern enclaves were generally good in April 1995 when some 82 per cent of the food target was met. UNHCR was also successful in gaining fairly regular access to the enclaves in early May. However, due to the deteriorating situation following the May air strikes, UNHCR was forced to cancel some convoys to Gorazde for security reasons while others were denied access by the Bosnian Serbs. Access to Srebrenica and Zepa was, however, unhindered. In June, UNHCR access to Srebrenica and Zepa has been sporadic: after a one month period, Zepa received its first convoy of 50 MT of mainly food supplies on 21 June, and after six months of clearance refusal, one convoy with shelter material reached Srebrenica. Srebrenica also received a number of food convoys in June which helped to alleviate the increasingly difficult food situation in the pocket (UNHCR was only able to meet some 30 per cent of the food aid target in June). So far, only one UNHCR convoy has got into the enclaves in July - a 64 MT convoy to Srebrenica on 4 July. There have been reports by the Bosnian Government about the death by starvation of 13 civilians in Srebrenica in the past week. UNHCR is not in a position to confirm these reports but their Srebrenica office assessment is that although the food situation is precarious, it has not reached a level where the population is facing malnutrition." Now before getting to the part about the condition of the population, this description of some material making it and some material not making it, is that generally, in your view, a fair reflection of what was allowed in to Srebrenica and the other areas discussed in this -- in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "a fair reflection" of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this look relatively accurate? I know it was a long time ago, but does this look to you to be a -- an relatively accurate or closely accurate account of the work you were doing, given your close involvement in these approvals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in giving approvals, rather in the drafting of certain documents when Colonel Djurdjic was not there so that something that had been approved could get through, but this information is relevant and I wouldn't want to give my comments on what Yasushi Akashi is writing. I hadn't received this information. I hadn't seen this. As for the dead, I am quite skeptical because in order to reach loftier objectives, we know that they were carrying out propaganda in order to get a military intervention. Died of hunger. No one died of hunger in this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 17806 will receive number P6861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we now go to 65 ter 04394.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we're waiting for this, sir, I can tell you this is a combat report from the army of the BH command, the 28th Division, in Srebrenica, in the name of their Chief of Staff Ramiz -- Major Ramiz Becirovic. And it's dated 6th July 1995 which is the same date as the UN document we saw. Now you may also recall that 6 July was the date that the attack by the VRS on the Srebrenica enclave began, just as a historical reference. So that first page where they are talking about the actions of the aggressor is not something I'm interested in with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go to the next page in the English and in the B/C/S. And if we could go under the situation of the -- the humanitarian situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would point out, and I think you'll agree, that this combat report is from the 28th Division to its own command. It's not to any international. It's to its own command. And let's look at -- see what they're telling their command about the humanitarian situation. And I quote under paragraph 4: "The situation continues to be exceptionally difficult. The food convoy announced for today has not arrived. Elderly and weak persons are in an exceptionally difficult situation due to starvation. The first people to die of hunger in the area of Srebrenica after the demilitarisation were registered today. I request that every effort be made to deliver food to our area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, now, I said several times today that you should speak at an non-audible volume. Now take that seriously because -- you can whisper if you want to consult with counsel, otherwise we will have to go back to the system with the little notes and that's not what you prefer, I think. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So again I'll ask you, were you getting intelligence reports or other information that you were able to intercept from the Muslims speaking to each other that indicated the people of Srebrenica were dieing of hunger, some people were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 04394 will be Exhibit P6862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now lastly I have one last document on a topic that you discussed yesterday and that is medical evacuations. So I want to take you to -- the year is now 1994 for a document that's dated 4 November 1994. And it has to do with a situation prior to that in July 1994, I believe. And we understand that you did not become part of the Main Staff until November 1994, but I recall you did tell us that you learned quite a bit about what had happened before from the documents there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could have 65 ter 3489 before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We can see from this that this is a report and it's just the front page of the report. And it, as we can see in the middle of that front paragraph, it's from the Special Rapporteur Tadeusz Mazowiecki on the human rights situation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. There is many pages to this document, but I am only interested in three, this first page, so you can see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then I want to go to page 22 in the B/C/S, page 17 in the English, entitled: "Interference with Humanitarian Aid and Assistance."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So looking at paragraph 65 down at the bottom. I won't read it at this point. We see, as we scan it briefly, it's talking about thefts from convoys, which is not something I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page. In the English it should be page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it notes at the top of the page: "Bosnian Serb de facto authorities have also interfered with humanitarian activities in Gorazde by their refusal to permit medical evacuation of seriously ill people by helicopter. On 21 July 1994, the Special Rapporteur issued a public appeal calling for the immediate reversal of an evacuation refusal which was endangering the lives of some 34 people. The Bosnian Serb de facto authorities eventually allowed an evacuation only on 5 October 1994, when 24 patients were taken from the enclave. The delay in giving consent resulted in the deaths of two patients." Now, I think we recall you earlier saying something to the effect that medical evacuations were allowed. This is obviously a very serious report on the horrible consequences of two people. Was this something that you had heard about when you arrived and started working on these issues?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for medical evacuations, it was much safer for these persons to travel by land. Helicopters are very sensitive and certain procedures had to be observed. They had to be announced and there was air control and landing and so on. For medical evacuation or for transporting UNPROFOR officials into the enclaves, when helicopters were used for these purposes, sometimes the Muslim forces would use the corridors allowed for their own helicopters. I saw some records to that effect. And once I had the opportunity of participating in checking a helicopter that was transporting officials from Sarajevo to Gorazde. It had been agreed that the helicopter was supposed to land at the airport, the Heliodrom, the football stadium in Sokolac. And it was checked when it arrived and when it left. So I don't understand. If it wasn't possible to be transported by helicopter, why didn't they ask for a land transportation? I'm also challenging these two victims. There are no names, surnames. Anything can be stated for propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now would you like to answer the question? Did you hear about this incident, this situation in this report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to offer, and under the guide-lines, just these three pages so you don't have this entire report. Though I have no objection if for context or for some reason they want the entire report, which I believe is 22 pages of some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're tendering at this moment these three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, we received -- actually, I received this document this morning at half past 8.00, but I do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the three pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are not uploaded separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll make an A of those pages so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we reserve a number for it. We don't have yet the A number, although we expect that it will be -- where are we? Yes, it's disappeared from my screen. But, Madam Registrar, what we have on our screen at this moment is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 3489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3489A, most likely, still to be uploaded, would receive what number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go now to 65 ter 31527 on this same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what you'll -- what you see here, you can see that that's the first page of the classic -- what we've already seen, a translated UN request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page. And page 2 in the B/C/S and in the English. I apologise. I believe we've -- we've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So within that translated UNPROFOR request, we see this reference. It's dated 19 July 1994, from UNPROFOR, entitled: "Helicopter medivac from Gorazde." "Could you please approve helicopter medivac of sick and wounded civilians from Gorazde to Sarajevo on Thursday, 21 July ..." Which as we saw was the date in the Mazowiecki report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should add 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "The BH Command received a letter from the Republika Srpska Army on 18 July," then it gives the number. "The response to this letter is being drafted and will be sent to you as soon as it is ready. However, this medical evacuation has to be done as soon as possible before some patients from the list die." And then it's handwritten: "But Serbs can die." Now, this Serbian version that -- that's a version that you in your team or someone in the Main Staff had translated so it can be properly considered; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would receive a copy of the English version and a copy of the translation from the office at Pale from the UNPROFOR military observers. We would just compare the translation to see whether it was correct and whether there were any typos on the facts and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you've already gone over similar documents like this where you identified General Mladic's signature. Isn't this a similar UNPROFOR request that you are looking at and people in the VRS are making handwritten notes on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be interested in what it is that you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Isn't this one of the requests that was considered by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see it handwritten at the top "ne," no. And with it handwritten: "All of it can be done by land if that is also approved."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the top of the page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To the far top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is in effect what you had mentioned when I showed you the previous report, that they should go by land. So can you tell us, do you recognise this handwriting where it says "ne" and "all of it can be done by land if that is also approved"? And then there is initials.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the initials of Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the handwriting that we see there, that "all of it can be done," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often he would write using the Latin script. It is his initials. Now, whether it is his handwriting, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the handwriting where it says, "But Serbs can die"? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- in this respect. You see on the top of the page in the B/C/S twice handwritten "ne," on the far left and in the middle. Was that a common practice, to put "ne" twice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not common practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I just -- on one question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I thought that you would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I'm following up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please, go ahead. Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31527 will receive Exhibit P6864.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6864 is admitted. Please put your next question to the witness, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These two "nes," can you tell are they the same initials, the same person? Or two different people writing "ne"? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. At the time I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So that's in evidence. Last document, Colonel Kralj, last questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have -- this -- sorry, it is the same document. It's just another page in it. Slightly confused on that. But it's page 1. And then if we could go to page 1, which is from the Main Staff to the UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are on page 1 of the document -- sorry, which document? Which document do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's -- that's where we want to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which document is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's now P6864. It's, as you recall, these -- these packets came in with the -- first it was the VRS response and then within those responses were copies of the UNPROFOR requests with the VRS notations on them. So now we're going to what the VRS, in the Prosecution's understanding, believe is a response regarding these various convoy requests. And we can see that it's a -- if you -- if we go to the next page, we'll see that it's in the name of Lieutenant-General Milovanovic. So let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see General Milovanovic saying to UNPROFOR on 20 July 1994, number 1: "Helicopter medical evacuation on 21 July 1994 from Gorazde to Sarajevo. We insist on equal treatment of the sick Serbs on the Muslim territory and the sick Muslims in the enclaves. We are waiting for your response that you are preparing." And when we look at this in combination to the handwritten note on that same -- on that related request that says "Serbs can die," is this an example of how the Main Staff dealt with these issues, not letting sick Muslims out until sick Serbs are out, playing with lives like that? Is this what it looks like?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks different to me. That sick people are supposed to be treated on the Muslim side as well and that UNPROFOR could assist this treatment on this territory, whereas they only care about Muslims in the enclaves and nobody cares about the Serbs, the sick Serbs in Muslim territory. Probably General Milovanovic had more information about this and that is why he acted in this way. Concrete information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, I'd offer this into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness specify. Could you tell us what specific information he had on just this item, that is the -- that is a number of civilians, as it was asked, to be evacuated by helicopter? What was the information he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say because I wasn't there at the time, and I know that they always asked that our people, who were in Sarajevo or in other places under Muslim control, should have appropriate care, receive proper medical care. They did not have that. When they would flee across the lines, they would say that they did not have any kind of care whatsoever, let alone medical care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, these were apparently people that still could cross lines, whereas we are talking about evacuation by helicopter of ill people here. Now you earlier, when asked about it without these details, you told us more or less that it required all kind of preparations and I think we see in the follow-up of this document, we see how the request was made, what details were given, et cetera, et cetera. Now, you gave us in earlier answers the impression that the Main Staff was very much willing to co-operate if proper procedures were followed, whereas the document we have now before us says, "No, we don't do it if you don't do the same." That is -- that has got nothing to do with preparations and safe landing, et cetera. It's just a -- if I could say, a political statement. If you don't do it, we'll not do it either. That's a different type of picture than you gave when answering previous questions. Could you explain why the documents depict a situation which is not -- seems not to be fully in line with what you told us in your previous answers? Now, it's the last time, Mr. Mladic. It's really, I'm -- you speak, either you have to wait until the break or you use notes. It's now the fifth time today that I have to say it to you and there is no need for that. You fully understand it. You should just do it. Witness, could you -- could you explain why the impression you give in your answers is quite different from what we see in this document and in other documents we've seen before about convoys and humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was an individual case. Every case was dealt with on its own and there could have been different influences. In this specific case, a possibility was considered to improve the situation of the sick and frail who were in the territory under Muslim control. I have no other explanation. And this is all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it sounds as if it's a general policy statement rather than a decision in an individual case. Was this the policy, not to evacuate sick if not certain conditions were met in the opposite direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not a general policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then explains that it's used here as an argument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "We are awaiting your answer." Obviously, there had been previous discussions about this topic, because it says that an answer is in the pipeline and is awaited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the line before it reads: "We insist on equal treatment of the sick Serbs on the Muslim territory and the sick Muslims in the enclaves." That sounds very much as a general policy statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no policy was within my purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. Mr. McCloskey, where are we as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This document, of course, is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pardon my confusion. And the excerpt pages from 65 ter 03489 have been assigned P06863. They've now been uploaded in e-court under 65 ter 03489A. And that ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is this 3489 or 4389?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, 03489A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A. Madam Registrar, I think we had reserved a number for it already. That was --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number reserved was P6863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Mr. Kralj, we take a break. We would like to see you back after the break for re-examination, if there is any need for re-examination. You may follow the usher. Well, you're doing it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, you'll be re-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, good morning once again.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P6855.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've seen this document, Mr. Kralj. It is dated 12 September 1992. It was issued by the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. There is a reference to Major Slavko Kralj, you. You were asked about this document, whether you had sent intelligence to your command. I would have a question about this document as well. Did UNPROFOR observers whom you escorted know that you reported back to your command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR observers did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how did they perceive your role? If you know, from conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew that my role was to receive them at the border crossing, since they arrived from Croatia, and to escort them along the route of the withdrawal of forces north of the Sava River where they were supposed to carry out controls in keeping with the agreements. I was their guide, their interpreter, their escort, and their security detail on that route. Having inspected the area, they returned to their original base in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up P1469.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is Directive 7. My learned friend McCloskey showed it to you yesterday. This is the cover letter sent by Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are interested in the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see here that the document was signed by President Radovan Karadzic. You told us that you didn't know anything about directives, but since you were shown this one, I'll try to deal with contestable parts very quickly. In this document we are interested in the page that the Prosecutor showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it would be page 14 and in B/C/S page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 6 is something that we will have to remember because we are going to see another document. I'm interested in 6.1, actually: "Moral and psychological support."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the following page or, rather, two pages further on, because there is one empty page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown that this directive says that: "Through the relevant stated military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, thus making them dependent on our good will while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." On yesterday's record, page 65, line 21, you said that General Ratko Mladic and Djuric were responsible for the implementation of this directive. [In English] Only it's Djurdjic. [Interpretation] And now let's look at Directive 7.1, drafted by General Ratko Mladic, concerning the implementation of this directive signed by President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in P1470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "drafted." Signed or drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not the same. You said it was drafted by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I -- I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it was drafted and signed by Mr. -- or it was signed by General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then you're giving -- you're giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll -- first I want to show the first page to the witness and then we'll see the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, what we have before us is a directive for further combat operations, operative number 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In keeping with the words of Judge Orie, let's look at the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise General Mladic's signature here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we need to go to page 5 in B/C/S and page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same part of the directive which concerns support for combat activities, again bullet point 6.1 which concerns moral and psychological support. Look at that part and then we'll move to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can please scroll down to the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, please look at the bottom of this page and then we will go to the following page. Did you read the bottom of the page under 6.1?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in the B/C/S version and scroll down to the bottom of the page in English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you done reading?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this Directive 7.1 which was written by General Mladic, did you come across the word from Directive 7 by President Karadzic; i.e., to restrict, reduce the logistical support by UNPROFOR and the supply to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this directive there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it took us five minutes to establish that those words do not appear in 7.1, which, irrespective of what conclusions you would draw from that, seems not to be in dispute between Prosecution and Defence, is it, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Therefore why do we need five minutes to establish that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because I objected yesterday that Mr. McCloskey was showing to this witness only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you put --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you put to the witness 7.1 and you say to the witness, "Mr. Witness, I put 7.1 now to you. The text which your attention was drawn to yesterday does not appear in this text." Prosecution and Defence agree on that. That takes 30 seconds and then you ask the questions you want to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you would say that I was leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I don't have the right to lead it -- lead him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if the parties agree on a matter -- and I think I'm insisting again and again and again to see what is in dispute and what is not in dispute and to focus what is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there is one thing which is not in dispute is that this text does not appear in 7.1 where it appears in 7. Am I wrong, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, that's always been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, 7.1 is in evidence so to that extent it would not be leading. It doesn't elicit any new evidence triggered by your pointing at this, so therefore don't waste time, Mr. Lukic. Be focused and try to get from this witness what you are seeking to get from him and not spend time on the issues as I explained it to you. Please put the questions to the witness which are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, we claim that the Prosecutor informed you only about Directive 7 yesterday. They didn't show you Directive 7.1. All the answers you provided about that excluded Directive 7.1. That's what I'm going to ask you. If there is Directive 7.1 which was signed by General Mladic, the Army of Republika Srpska and you personally, do you comply with Directive 7 which was signed by President Karadzic or do you comply with Directive 7.1 which was signed by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS and I personally would comply with directives, i.e. orders, issued by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the implementation of Directive 7 was in the hands of General Mladic. Was Directive 7.1 the way for him to implement the directive that he had received from President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the way to write General Mladic's units, directives based on President Karadzic's directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let me try to put a primarily relevant question to the witness. Having established that the text about the convoys about the humanitarian aid does not appear in 7.1 signed by Mr. Mladic, where it does appear in Directive 7, do you know why that text does not appear in 7.1 where it did appear in Directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now take a look at P6857.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown this conversation. You say that it took place between Mr. Obucina and General Tolimir. Mr. Obucina says he asked you about that exchange for Srebrenica. Were some humanitarian aid exchanged with Srebrenica or does this have to do with something else? This text, does it have anything to do with humanitarian aid? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cannot be seen, that this has to do with humanitarian aid. Exchanges often took place in respect of military observers who were in safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Were prisoners exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were exchanges of prisoners, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look at document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in relation to this. On the 23rd of June, 1995, was there any exchange of prisoners being prepared at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners exchanged in, well, let's say, the weeks following the 23rd of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was Milos in this conversation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos was the chief of the sector for civilian affairs and a member of the state co-ordination body for humanitarian co-operation, and within that body there was another member who dealt with the subject of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was Milos in any way involved and was this committee directly involved in the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had a person who carried out prisoner exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be seen there in that document. I cannot recall, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the -- which document do you exactly mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the decision on the establishment of the state co-ordination body of March 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you give the full name of Milos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you get anything out of your pocket -- Mr. Kralj, you're not supposed to use any notes of yours here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's not correct. And people have been allowed to review their notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to refresh their recollection, and so directing something like that is not his position in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, but never without the approval of the Chamber. To that extent, I would say Mr. Lukic is perfectly right. Perhaps the most elegant way of dealing with it, before you do this, could you tell us what you intend to be shown and then ask the Chamber for permission. That's the elegant way to deal with it, but basically I understand your observation. You wanted to stop the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- without permission to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, the Prosecution would like to see what he had in his pocket as you might also understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are not usually doing searches in pockets of witnesses, but let's -- let me -- Mr. Kralj, but what kind of document or piece of paper did you want to consult when you took it out of your pocket? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I had the name of that person who was in the co-ordination body and who was in charge of the exchange of prisoners. I think that I had it written down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For any specific purpose that you have it with you here, or do you have a list of things that you should not forget about or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply so that I wouldn't forget if I'm asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. I can deal with this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll leave it to that. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, this is going to take up a bit of our time, but if you are consulting something -- I mean, I don't know what it is that you have. We will have to hand that over to the Prosecution, then.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I give up on showing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us see D366, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps while waiting for that, I would like to seek one matter. I asked you, Witness, whether Milos was in any way involved in the exchange of prisoners and whether the committee was, and your answer was: "He was involved." Was the committee involved in the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The committee was involved in the exchange of prisoners, and Milos was supposed to secure unhindered passage in agreement with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I misspoke. It should be D336. [Interpretation] So this is the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. And on the next page in the B/C/S version, and the third page of the English version. Perhaps -- actually the fourth page in the English version. [In English] Everything is not translated. Let's try with the second page. Well, then, the first page. Maybe only this is translated into English. That's the correct page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see a decision here on forming a state committee for co-operation with the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. You've mentioned mid-March 1995 a moment ago. As regards this committee, yesterday you saw that Dr. Nikola Koljevic was the chairman of this committee, that Maksim Stanisic was the deputy chairman, and then there were nine members that were listed. Did you ever attend meetings of this body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the work of that body, and with Colonel Milos I visited the premises and took part in one session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see how this body reached its decisions? Did they take a vote? Could you explain that to us? Could you tell us how the decision-making took place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Majority vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Colonel Milos Djurdjic, I assume, had one vote?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are done with this document. Could we now take a look at P6860, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document? You have already seen it today. The date is the 14th of June, 1995. At this time, that is to say, June 1995, were Serb positions already bombed by NATO forces -- or, rather, May 1995. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bombing started at the end of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment, did the Serb side believe that UNPROFOR had sided with the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was UNPROFOR informed even before the bombing that if bombing does take place they would be considered to be the enemy party?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was UNPROFOR informed after the bombing started that the Serb side considered them to be an enemy in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not considered to be the enemy until the very beginning of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb side have any information to the effect that within UNPROFOR there were people who were navigating NATO air strikes, leading them to Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side had intelligence to the effect that in the territory there were people who could and were equipped to guide NATO aircraft so that they could hit targets as precisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I take you back to one of my questions I asked you a while ago; that is, whether the Main Staff considered UNPROFOR to be the enemy in terms of the armed conflict. You then said no. I now do understand that on from a certain point in time they did, so your previous answer was at least not the whole of the truth. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was the truth, but the situation on the ground led UNPROFOR to the position of a party to the conflict once the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means, therefore, that your answer was part of the truth because it's valid only for a certain period of time and not, when the question was asked without any restrictions, is not a complete answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the same time, what about UNPROFOR rapid deployment forces? Did they bomb the Serb side? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it UNPROFOR, Mr. Lukic, that bombed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's part of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rapid force. On Mount Igman. Rapid force, it was part of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although this position had been taken, did the VRS and the Main Staff of the VRS continue to co-operate with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was normalised and normal co-operation continued after a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What time does the witness have on his mind? Was this after the Srebrenica take-over or before the take-over of Srebrenica that the situation was normalised again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the take-over of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although NATO bombarded Serbian positions with UNPROFOR's help, was humanitarian aid delivered to the enclaves in May and June?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid did arrive both in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's see P6860, please. [In English] P6861.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again we can see a UN report which was sent to Mr. Annan in New York. My learned friend showed you bullet point 4 in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would therefore kindly ask the same page to be displayed on the screen now. [In English] So it's the next page in B/C/S as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report itself, although we don't have it on the screen -- oh, no, we do have it. It says UNHCR was forced to cancelled some convoys to Gorazde for security reasons, while others were denied access by the Bosnian Serbs. In June, UNHCR access to Srebrenica and Zepa has been sporadic. Did you in the Main Staff know, were you privy to the information that the Muslim side in Srebrenica reported over 40.000 people residing in Srebrenica? As a matter of fact, the real number was about 34.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are concerned about being blamed for leading, Mr. Lukic, you whisper already the answer in the ears of the witness, isn't it? That's what we call leading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could ask the witness whether he has any knowledge about the number of the population being reported by the Muslims. You could ask that. If he knows, he can tell us. Witness, did you have access to any information provided by the Muslims about the number of people living in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have access to that information then. I only learnt that here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report is dated 6 July 1995. It was compiled on the 6th of July, 1995, in New York. It says in this report, towards the end of bullet point 4 in the last quarter of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll need the next page in B/C/S version. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you say this was a document drafted in New York. From what I read, it is sent by Akashi to Annan --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ah, to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that Akashi is located in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Zagreb. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's an important matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a hidden way of leading as well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, I apologise. I misspoke. The document was drafted on the 6th of July, 1995, by Mr. Akashi in Zagreb. It says in the report: The Bosnian government was informed about 13 civilians in Srebrenica in -- who died of starvation last week. Well, that was in June, that's when the first people died of starvation. You said that the Muslim side used that as propaganda and that you did not believe such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up the following document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor, and that was P6862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again, if a document is dated the 6th of July and if people died the last week, 13, then that's not in June, that is mainly in July and perhaps to some extent in June. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are giving interpretation -- last week, that is the week --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the 6th. Last week from the 6th starts seven days before or ends 14 days before that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I at least understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand "last week" to mean the seven days before the date when --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a document is -- what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least. At least seven days before. Or 14, 14 days before. It's last week anyways and we'll see what the next document says on that topic, the document that is in front of us. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- composed by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslim side, on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's first try to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I write something on the 6th of July and I'm talking about the last week, my understanding is that that's the seven days preceding the 6th of July. Would we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even if I agree with that, I don't have to change my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said it was in June, whereas for me it's at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- five days in July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same day, 6th of July, we have another document composed by the Army of B&H.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, the date is 6th July 1995 and the time is 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are interested in the last page in both versions of the document, bullet point 4, and the title is: "Humanitarian Situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read so you don't have to if the letters are too small. "The situation continues to be exceptionally difficult. The food convoy announced for today has not arrived." This is the day when combat started as you could see in the first sentence of the document. "The elderly and the frail are in an exceptionally difficult situation due to starvation. The first people to die of hunger in the area of Srebrenica after the demilitarisation were recorded today." Again, no names of those who allegedly starved to death. Would you agree with me -- or rather, in your view, does this document contradict the one that was sent out by Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not a question for the witness. That's a question that, whether it contradicts or not, is an interpretation of a text. If the witness knows anything about those who died and when they died, we'd like to hear that. But whether one document which is not written by the witness contradicts another document which is not written by the witness either is not a question you'd put to a witness. It's a matter which may be argued among the parties but is not a matter of knowledge of facts. Please proceed. And we could ask the witness whether he knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, do you know of anybody who starved to death in Srebrenica on the 6th of July or thereafter? Obviously according to Ramiz Becirovic, before that day from the moment the enclave was demilitarised nobody died of starvation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Lukic, you are giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in this document [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the document says that it was registered on that day. To die on one day and to register that death as caused by a certain event is not the same. You can ask the witness whether he knows anything about people dying from starvation. If he knows anything and about details, he could tell us. But it's now the second question which is -- first of all, the first question was one you couldn't put to the witness. The second one now is misrepresenting the evidence. Would you please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received by another witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- provided by the Prosecution that there is no any kind of register of death in Srebrenica, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That means that then the document is false because registration --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If there is any register of deceased, we would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are not discussing at this moment other evidence, that's argument not for the witness. Please put your next question to the witness and refrain from further discussing the matter in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that deaths from starvation were recorded in Srebrenica on the 6th of July or before that or after that, on any date for that matter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that deaths from starvation were recorded in Srebrenica. This is nothing but propaganda that they engaged in very often in order to get as much humanitarian aid as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whether it's propaganda or not was first of all not asked; and second, is opinion rather than observation of facts. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. My client just asked, which is -- I don't remember ever happened, that he has to leave the courtroom for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have either regular break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's time -- break time anyways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you still need, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not much. I have to see two more documents so probably five, six minutes. But we have to interrupt now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll do that after the break. But would you carefully consider the type of questions that you are putting to the witness and to stay well within defined lines of what is appropriate to ask in re-examination and what is not. We take a break. The witness can follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to come in, the Chamber has received the joint submission of the parties regarding the notebooks of Milenko Indjic. The parties have agreed, at least suggested, that the Chamber orders that the notebooks be returned to Witness Indjic and that Mr. Indjic may be released as a witness in this case. The Chamber follows that suggestion, which means that the Registrar -- the Registry is hereby instructed to return the notebooks to Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that Mr. Indjic be informed that he is released as a witness in this case. Mr. Lukic, we'll be rather strict on time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'm going to read out that last question of mine, when you included propaganda in your answer, and what I asked you was whether you knew that there were any deaths from hunger in Srebrenica on the 6th of July, before that, after that. That's on page 44, line 10. And in line 13 you said: "I do not know of any starvations being recorded in Srebrenica." This is what I'd like to ask you: The representatives of UNPROFOR, did they ever submit any documents to you stating that someone had died in Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Tuzla, died of hunger?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In document P6863, something was put to you in relation to the 21st of July, 1994; namely, that evacuation of persons had been prevented. And that was also supported by document P6864.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at this document in e-court, P6864.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that General Milovanovic in his letter to UNPROFOR, dated the 20th of July, says in paragraph 1 -- actually, before that, before the numbers, he said: "We hereby inform you that we did not approve the movements of UNPROFOR teams and convoys as follows:" And it says here: "Helicopter medical evacuation on the 21st of July, 1994, from Gorazde to Sarajevo." After that there is another sentence: "We insist on equal treatment of the sick Serbs on the Muslim territory and the sick Muslims in the enclaves." Were you told that UNPROFOR should act equally towards the Serb side and the opposing side? How did you understand the role of UNPROFOR in that respect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR is supposed to be neutral and to treat the parties to the conflict in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at a document that the Prosecution said they would use during your cross-examination but they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 31526, that's the 65 ter number. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think announcements are always what parties may use during examination or cross-examination and not what they will use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say you "would use."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not on my list, that's why I wanted to give the explanation why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, first of all, you don't have to explain anything of the kind to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] This is a document where it says that it was sent from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 22nd of July, 1994. Could we take a look at the last page.
