utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see a stamp here. Also we see the name of Manojlo Milovanovic typed out. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the signature of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first sentence says: "I have received your letter and" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see page 1 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour. In both versions we need the first page, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In respect of medical evacuation, paragraph 1 reads as follows: "Your evaluation of the medical evacuation was that there were successes and there was a lack of success, that is to say, that there was co-operation and that there was a lack thereof." Further on, General Milovanovic says: [As read] "I regret that you did not completely clarify your conclusion and that I am forced to do so myself. "Medical evacuations were always successful when we were the ones who approved evacuation of Muslims; however, whenever we requested evacuation of Serbs, you did not accept that and evacuation was not successful. Therefore, the problem lies in your different treatment of the parties to the conflict." General Milovanovic goes on to explain that. But now we are going to skip over to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is on the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what paragraph 4 says: "Your claim that medical evacuations from the areas surrounded by the Army of Republika Srpska have been repeatedly prevented is not true. You have no evidence of that and that is why you were not able to present it. You probably do not have information about how many humanitarian acts Serbs carried out in relation to Muslims and Croats. I would be extremely glad if you were to ask Muslims and Croats to treat Serbs in the same way as Serbs treat them." And then in paragraph 6 it says, referring to the letter of the other side, UNPROFOR: "In item 9, you admit that UNPROFOR does not do enough for Serbs." Towards the end of this paragraph, it says: "UNPROFOR has access to Serbs on the territory under the control of the Muslims and the Croats and the VRS" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- "does not hinder you in any way in that respect."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with this topic and this letter that General Milovanovic is sending to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo to Colonel Kofret [phoen]. Do you know -- do you personally know, do you have any experience to that effect, that Serbs asked for the humanitarian evacuation of Serbs from territory that was held by Muslim and Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Lukic, if you would have put this question five minutes ago to the witness without reading the whole of the document, then we would have really stayed within the five or six minutes you announced. We are now -- I don't know whether you have -- if you have one more question, you can put it to the witness, but you have wasted most of your time and most of the time of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that we wasted the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, I'm not inviting you to comment on that. It is established unanimously by this Chamber during the break that the time you used in re-examination was mainly wasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you point so I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in future what was wasted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I want you to put your last question to the witness and I don't want to enter into a further debate with you on the matter. This is not a debating club. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it the policy of the VRS, of its Main Staff, not to allow medical evacuations and not to allow civilians to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that was your last question, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would introduce this document to evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31526 will be Exhibit D729.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D729 is admitted. Any further questions, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could ask, Mr. President, there was a -- in regard to the intercept with Obucina, there was a challenge suggesting that was a or could be an exchange of prisoners. I would like to get into that topic if that would be of help to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to be a matter which was in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I -- if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. If I may clarify, the witness said he knows nothing about the exchange of the prisoners but he thinks that's an exchange or rotation of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no reason for you to repeat how you understood what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have heard the testimony of the witness. There was clearly a difference in interpretation and understanding of this document and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After a clarification, Your Honour, it's not our understanding anymore that it can deal with exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, if we could -- we've identified what is likely a translation error in the word "exchange," that may help clear it up. And if the Defence will agree that this has to do with the rotation of humanitarian workers, then I'd -- I can sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you more or less stipulated what it is not, that it's not about an exchange of prisoners. Now Mr. McCloskey invites you to agree on what it then was. I don't know whether you would agree to that as well but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have the answer of the witness. He thinks that's it's a rotation of UNMOs. But to be honest with you, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, not that I don't think so, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what the witness thinks, as a matter of fact, is not of great probative value, but if you do not agree that it is and if you say it's what the witness thinks it may be is not yet or not the position of the Defence, then Mr. McCloskey will ask some further questions on the matter, I take it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, the rotation of UNMOs, the United Nations Military Observers, does that fit under the category of humanitarian topics or is that more of an UNPROFOR issue?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It pertains to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So since you've mentioned that this intercept --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which is P -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get you that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P6857, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've mentioned to us, and we'll all remember, that you felt that this was a discussion with the -- about the co-ordinating body for the humanitarian issues. So let's go to one more intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 25112. And I want -- hopefully I'll have the transcript of this intercept on the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll see that it's a 23 June intercept. We unfortunately don't have the times, so we can't compare that. But we'll remember that 23 June was the date of the subject intercept that we had just talked about. And we see that this one is a conversation between Petko Obucina and Colonel Milos Djurdjic. And you have told us about who those folks are. And just so everyone knows, Colonel Djurdjic is deceased; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this early on in -- an unknown man says: "Yes." And Petko says: "Milos, it's me again." And the unknown man says: "Who are you?" And Petko says: "Ah, it's ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The transcription was done by the Miletic Defence team, Your Honour, I'm sorry. We haven't corrected that. Your Honour, that should be ignored as well. Unknown man: "Greetings, sir." And Petko says: "What's up Mr. ...?" The unknown man says: "Hello. Well, my boss is busy on the other line." Petko says: "Busy?" "Yes, yes." And then finally Milos Djurdjic gets on the line and says: "Yes?" Petko says: "I just spoke to the General." Milos Djurdjic has a question: "Which one?" And Petko says: "Tolimir." Djurdjic says: "Where?" "On 154." Can we go to the next page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you do recall the previous conversation was between -- Tolimir was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's go also in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we go down and we see that Petko says: "He said: If Milos didn't, like he didn't understand it well, the main boss said that they can go to Srebrenica and they should go and come out." Milos says: "Yes." And Petko says: "And he said, we will tell Milos that." Milos says: "Good." Petko says: "And he told me to tell the professor that it's okay." That would be Professor Koljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Milos says: "Good." Petko says: "Well, could you please ..." Milos says: "I'll wait for them to tell me that." Petko says: "Good. Look, could I ask you something ..." Milos says: "Just don't ... have them rotate tomorrow, for God's sake." Petko says: "Have them what? Djurdjic says: "Have them rotate tomorrow." Petko says: "... for tomorrow there's a notification, as far as I remember." And we can follow it down the rest of the way. Milos says: "Well, I have to see with ... talk to Tosa." Tosa is Tolimir, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did your office handle the rotations of the staff of MSF, Doctors Without Borders, into and out of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone and everything that entered Srebrenica and that left Srebrenica was within Milos's line of work, MSF included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in looking at these intercepts together, do they appear related to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are related.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was translated "if they have any connection with each other," and Mr. McCloskey asked "any connection with you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's why the answer was: "They are related," but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the answer would be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- yes, are the two conversations as recorded, are they related or did you intend to say that they were related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two conversations are related, the conversations, because they deal with the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I was incorrect when I thought the intercept transcript was from the Miletic Defence team. It was not. It was our own translation that we had received from others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it that you'll remove any suggestive remarks in it which you did not read and which you already said should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if I may, if you are going to -- if my learned friend is finished with this document, I have an intervention regarding the document as well. In crucial part it's not correctly translated in English document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then it means --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that both --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I could read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there is a translation issue and there is an issue with interpretative remarks in the document which shouldn't be there. I'd suggest that -- do you intend to tender it Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- McCloskey? Yes. Then I'd suggest that we just reserve a number for the time being, not doing anything else, and it's about this intercept which certainly will not go in as it is now. Madam Registrar, the number for the intercept still to be reviewed, intercept 23rd of June, 1995, speaking Obucina and Djurdjic, would be what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P6865, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would suggest, Mr. Lukic, that this number now being reserved, that you tell Mr. McCloskey what your concerns are as far as the translation is concerned. Then we hear from the parties later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we can work that out. So I -- one last document on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go to the last document, Mr. McCloskey, it looks like your question was not answered. You asked whether these documents were related to the witness, the witness answered the question are they related to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you -- having been able to study these documents, can you put yourself -- do you have any memory of yourself of this -- of being involved in these in any way, being on the -- on the phone or involved or with knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I picked up the phone. I said to Obucina that Milos was on another line and I actually gave the receiver, the telephone to Colonel Djurdjic. As for the rest of the conversation, I am not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could we then just -- going through the text, it starts with Obucina saying, "Milos, it's me again," and then an unknown person says, "Who are you?" And then Obucina says, "I, it's" -- and apparently you are speaking at that moment? You are the unknown man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then we don't need it in the document but it's in evidence by other means, that the person speaking is Mr. Kralj before giving the phone to Milos. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll fix these. And I guess we can get rid of the question mark and the parentheses then, but we'll get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have it in evidence. It's not part of the conversation. So it should be taken out. But the Chamber heard evidence that the person speaking not identifying himself, in court has told us that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So this is in evidence. So let me go to one last document on a similar issue. It's P2156.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for that to come up, I can tell you that this is -- it is one of the Main Staff convoy issues related to humanitarian convoys. It's in the name of General Miletic which is on the second page. And this is dated 12 June, so I am not suggesting that it is associated necessarily one way or another what we've seen in the last two conversations. My question is: Is this as we see this, where they are -- the Main Staff we can see is agreeing with authorisations number 1382 MSF pertaining to members of its organisation exiting Srebrenica. But it goes on and makes clear that this is only the exit of the following persons from the area. Is this an example of the way the Main Staff dealt with MSF's request to enter and exit the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the date of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think the witness didn't limit himself to a certain period when he said that everything that went in and out, perhaps apart from him being at the Main Staff, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous document was for the 23rd June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- was my point. I don't know if this is related. I'm using this, as I said, as an example. If this witness can give it -- tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the question therefore is where you earlier testified that whatever came in and went out was -- had to be approved, that you said that MSF was not excluded from that general rule, to say so, whether this is an example of such a decision on whether or not MSF people could in this case leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I wonder, as a matter of fact, what's the use at all of such a question. I mean, it's logic rather than anything else, but I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you like answer to that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's a -- let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, we see at the bottom of this document in English: "In other words, no foreign MSF officials shall be allowed to enter the enclaves," on the next page, "except for, perhaps, drivers who will transfer the above-mentioned persons to Belgrade." This Court has heard evidence that during this period the -- from roughly March through July 1995, that rotations of international personnel many times were allowed to leave but were not allowed to come back. Were you aware of this, that many times international folks, be they UNPROFOR, MSF, UNMOs, or others, were allowed to leave the enclave but were not allowed to come back or be replaced?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Since the Chamber also has no further questions for you, Mr. Kralj, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, first of all, and then for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. It would be Dr. Veljko Maric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that the usher will escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, you are leaving. You'll be replaced by?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will -- I will stick around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll stick around. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Ms. Melikian would be able to leave, that would be how we're going to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One procedural matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- before the witness enters. Yesterday our 65 ter 1D2223 was MFI'd as D721. There was an error in the English translation. The B/C/S document was dated 2nd of May, 1994, but the English translation showed the date of 2nd of May, 1995. The OTP sent the document back -- back to CLSS asking that they revise the English translation to correct the date. The new corrected English translation of the D721 MFI'd has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D17-2058. So the Defence would seek permission to replace the English translation currently in the e-court with the new corrected English translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar is hereby instructed to replace the present English translation by the one -- the new one just mentioned by Mr. Lukic, the new doc ID being 1D17-2058. And there are no objections to admission, I think, therefore -- but, Madam Registrar, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I could kindly ask Defence counsel to release the document in -- the translation in e-court so it could be attached accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist, I'm told by our back room that actually the doc ID number is 1D17-0258, and that should be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I give a new instruction to Madam Registrar; that is, to replace the present English translation by the new one provided under number 1D17-0258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And D721 is admitted into evidence. Good afternoon, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, I would like to invite you to make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Maric. Mr. Maric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find him to your left, he's standing. And Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Can you please state your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Veljko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would ask that you be shown 65 ter number 1D4414 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we can see this is a witness statement from the Karadzic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could please take a look at the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask you, sir, if you could identify for us who is -- whose signature appears on the Serbian original at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: This is my signature. I signed the document on the 16th of March, 2013.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, subsequent to signing this statement in the Karadzic case, did you have occasion to review and read the same in the Serbian language to ascertain if everything is correct therein?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The opportunity was given to me, I read it, and I have objections to three paragraphs. I would like to clarify certain things. I would like to expand, if necessary, I would like to expand on those three paragraphs in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will go through them. First, sir, I'd like to take a look at paragraph number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that should be on the first page of the statement in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in paragraph 2 where you talk about the outpatient clinics of the Foca hospital, what corrections would you like to make?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The hospital in Foca has several outpatient clinics in Miljevina, Celebici, Godjenje, Tjentiste, and Ustikolina, whereas Gorazde is not an outpatients' clinic. It is the medical centre of Gorazde. In Bosnia, every municipality has its medical centre, Kalinovik, Cajnice, Rudo, Visegrad, Rogatica. They all belong to the Foca hospital but they are different organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could look at paragraph 4 which is also on the first page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any corrections that you wish to make in relation to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: On line 1 it says, "Before the war in Bosnia." I would like to add the word "Herzegovina." I don't know why it was omitted in the first place, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could take a look together at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is at the bottom of this page in both languages and then continues on to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What correction or corrections would you like to make to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: After the conflict which happened on the 8th of April, 1992, the Foca hospital was abandoned by specialists, a total of 32 of them. The hospital was left with fewer than 20 specialists in 17 different departments. Of the 32 specialists who abandoned the hospital after the 8th of April, 1992, belonged to all ethnic groups, fifteen were Muslims and seventeen specialists were Serbs. They abandoned the Foca hospital due to the conflict that happened on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you refer to paragraph 35. In my view the statement has only 26 -- sorry, Mr. Ivetic. The statement has only 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're too used to correct me. So it's Mr. Ivetic today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, but I'm happy that I first realised that I made the mistake. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I misspoke. We are relating to paragraph 5 which is at the bottom of page 1 and leads on to the top of page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one more clarification, Doctor. You mention specialists. Could you be more specific as to what -- what type -- what is a specialist? In what -- in what bases are you using that term?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: All hospitals have specialists, surgeons, anesthesiologists, specialists in internal medicine, pediatricians, and so on and so forth. They are all specialists in their respective fields of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now apart from these three corrections and additional information that you've provided, do you stand by everything as recorded in your written statement and given to the Karadzic case as being correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today questions on the same topics as contained in your statement, would your answers in substance be the same?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Given that you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth today, would those answers as contained in your statement be truthful?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, providing my corrections were included into the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would tender the statement which is 1D4414, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D4414 will be Exhibit D730.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D730 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, there are also three associated exhibits that I would tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there were some objections to those or the length, if I remember well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our position that those are not inseparable and indispensable to the statement, but we would have no objection to them being led through the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do you insist on having them admitted as associated exhibits or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do since they were covered in two paragraphs for each of the documents. I think the statement does sufficiently discuss the documents and they are integral to what is contained in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, could you explain a little bit more? I saw it in the response, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Our position is simply that referencing the document in the statement doesn't make them inseparable and indispensable, and in this case, we don't think that they meet the standard required for admission as associated exhibits. But we leave it in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could be corrected, the first document, which was 1D7238 in the Karadzic case and which is in our case 1D4415, is discussed at length in three paragraphs of the statement. I believe that is the criteria for a document to be considered integral. I'd be interested to know what other criteria is being cited by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph exactly, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. It's in paragraphs 11, 12, and 21 of the witness's statement, that that one document is discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I see that. And the document is a -- is that a list of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: List of patients, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: List of patients. Do we need, I do understand, 33 pages of lists of patients in order to establish that they are of all ethnicities? I mean, the problem is that the Chamber if it receives 33 pages, it has the habit of looking at all those pages to see whether it -- but if there is no disagreement between the parties that documents do show that patients of the various ethnicities were treated, then I think we can deal without. To that extent, you could ask yourself whether it's indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, Your Honours have indicated in your guidance a certain number of documents per statement that are permitted as associated exhibits. We are well under that with this statement which is only asking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not about numbers. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is. That's what the guidance was, Your Honours. It was number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the guidance was not only about the number. Of course, the Chamber has said that if documents would qualify as associated exhibits, and indispensability was one of the criteria for that, that if they would qualify, that nevertheless the Chamber would limit the number. So Ms. Harbour is not saying you are presenting too many, she's saying it's not indispensable. And I'm trying to find out whether the whole of the document, 33 pages, is indispensable in order to understand the testimony of this witness. Now, if there is no dispute about lists showing that patients were treated of various ethnicities, then I would say we could perfectly understand the evidence of this witness without going through those 33 pages. That is my point. And I'm looking at Ms. Harbour, is there any dispute about that those lists would show that various ethnicities were treated?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually the lists do not indicate the ethnicities of the patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not by names --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because often there is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: They list the patients' names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- so if one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Often names are indicative for ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Right. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about -- okay, if it's not the list, is there any dispute about persons of various ethnicities being treated in the hospital during the period of time as the lists are covering?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No, we don't dispute that persons of various ethnicities were patients at the hospital during this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at the time would be when? Could the parties agree on what are the times covered by the documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would be happy to agree with the time-period covered. It's quite clear from the documents which -- what the time-period is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's from April 1992 through the end of 1992, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: For one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no dispute about that matter, and we can understand the evidence of this witness even without looking at those lists. Therefore, the Chamber will further consider whether they are indispensable, yes or no. If the parties would make -- want to make any further submissions on that matter, because that's the issue, then they are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The one -- there is one document that relates to 1993 which is a list of Bosnian Muslim children that were cared for at the hospital and then sent to another facility in Montenegro in 1993. I don't know whether counsel has an objection to that or whether they stipulate to that being as stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think, as a matter of fact, that the witness explains in his statement about what happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so you can understand that even without if that's -- is that beyond dispute or?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the crux of our position, which is that the statement is understandable without the documents. But, again, we have no objection whatsoever to the Defence using these documents and tendering them through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. At the same time, of course, it's only needed if it's a matter which is in dispute. If there is no dispute about these matters, then we just can rely on the -- on the statement of the witness and we do not need all the supporting evidence, which is lengthy. So therefore, I'd suggest that the parties further -- for the lists of patients in relation to the admission of patients of different ethnicities there, it seems that we'll consider whether this is indispensable at all. And for the last list I leave it at this moment to the parties. We'll not yet decide on that. The statement itself, of course, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it already got a number, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think -- have we admitted it already in evidence or not? I have to check that. D730, if it was not yet admitted into evidence, is now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I have one more document that we have just put into e-court at the suggestion of the Prosecution. It's 1D05232. It's a table correlating the adjudicated facts from the Karadzic case to those in our case so that the references to adjudicated facts in the statement can be connected to those in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it then that there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D05232 will be Exhibit D731. And, Your Honours, if the document could be released in e-court as I don't see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will make that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D731, once released, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have a short summary of the statement pursuant to our practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just looking at the clock, Mr. Ivetic, and I'm wondering whether we should not first take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's take the break. That's probably easiest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you'll -- you asked for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was inclusive the tendering of the statement, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness, perhaps we can use the time. I've been now in contact with Prosecution counsel and the Prosecution indicated that we should identify the time-periods for the documents that are at issue: 1D4415, the parties stipulate that the documents relate to patients from the end of March through December of 1992; 1D4416, the parties stipulate that the documents relate to patients from April to May 1992; 1D4417, the parties stipulate that the records begin in January 1991 and contains entries through 1993, with the dates of birth indicating that these are children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those stipulations make the content of the statement well understandable, and therefore we do not need the lists. Is that -- is that the conclusion the parties could reach as well? Or is there any other reason why they are still to be considered as indispensable for understanding the statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Unless the Prosecution wants to cross-examine on the lists at all, I don't know. We didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I can imagine that that -- that that would cause you to present them as evidence. Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We do plan to cross-examine on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I then suggest that we wait until we've heard the cross-examination, that you reserve your right to use them because the Chamber would then be better able to understand the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We were at the point of the summary, which I begin. Dr. Veljko Maric is a surgeon who since 1993 has been the director of the Foca hospital. Dr. Maric states that the hospital in Foca town is the only hospital in Foca municipality. The hospital had a mixed hospital staff until the middle of July 1992, when Muslim staff and some Serb staff left the hospital due to the conflict. Both doctors who wished to leave and patients who needed dialysis were sent via hospital ambulances to Podgorica and Belgrade. In the early days due to fighting, the road from the hospital to Foca was blocked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down a bit, otherwise it's very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And only the road going to Montenegro by way of Celebici was usable. The doctor recalls that on 8 April 1992, the Green Berets prevented a bus carrying hospital staff from passing and the staff had to continue the rest of the way on foot. During the war, the Foca hospital treated persons of all ethnicities, including wounded persons and several children who were at the hospital, all the way until 1993 when they were sent to Igalo in Montenegro. The Foca hospital had tried to arrange to send these children to the Bosnian Muslim authorities but this gesture was refused. The military and civilian authorities in Foca had no influence over the running of Foca hospital. The health care system at the penal and correctional facility was separate and apart from the health care system of the hospital. However, during the war, doctors from the hospital would go to the KPD to treat the prisoners when needed and prisoners who needed extra treatment came to the hospital when needed. The doctor does not believe there was any discrimination of patients at the KPD based on ethnicity or religious affiliation. And that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. If you have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, first of all, I'd like to look at 1D4417 with you. This is identified in your statement as a list of children who were sent to Igalo. And I'd like to ask you, sir, based upon your knowledge of the patients and these records, could you identify for us what is the ethnicity or what are the ethnicities of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, it's 1D4417.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are children. From number 1 to number 3, they are children of Muslim ethnicity. 4, Simovic is of Serb ethnicity. Then 7 -- and 7 -- from 7, 8, 8 is Azra Ramovic, Muslim. And then 9 and 10 are Serb children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now take a look at D730.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is your written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd look to look at paragraph 12, which is on page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you state that every person that came to the hospital and sought treatment was treated irrespective of ethnicity, religion, or skin colour. Do you have any figures or statistics to demonstrate the number of ethnic Bosnian Muslim patients who were treated during the entirety of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The town of Foca or the municipality of Foca has a tradition of hospitals, because the first hospital was opened as early as 1896. This hospital that is 2 and a half kilometres away from the town, downstream on the right bank of the Drina river, was opened in 1958 and it has been working since then and is rendering services to this day. I have been the director over the past 20 years. I've been the director of this medical institution. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I stop you there. You are giving us now the history of the hospital and yourself, whereas the question was whether you could give us a number, statistics which would demonstrate the number of ethnic Bosnian Muslim patients treated during 1992. Could you please focus your answer on that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from the 8th of April, 1992, until the end, the 31st of December, roughly, in the hospital over 1.900 patients were treated. Out of this figure, about 300 patients were persons belonging to the Muslim people. And then, at the time, in that period, 22 children were born, Muslim children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. We have heard now the number 300 out of 1900. Wait for the next question. Whether Mr. Ivetic is interested in babies born or elderly being treated, I don't know yet what his next question would be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We've heard about children. Were there any other -- were there any other patients that are not included in the 3 00, in addition to the 22 children that were born, that were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, we also had seven children who were admitted, treated, and released, but they could not be taken to their families. Therefore, we kept them until the 29th of December, 1993. That is when, together with the Norwegian Red Cross, I managed to put these children up at the Dr. Simo Milosevic Hospital in Montenegro, in Igalo, and from there these children were reunited with their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask for clarification here. Doctor, in the summary that was read to us of your testimony, it was mentioned that the hospital tried to transport some children to the Muslim authorities but that this gesture was refused. By whom was this gesture refused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We tried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whom was it refused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Foca hospital to the border, there is about 10 kilometres to the Osanica line. So we took the children to Osanica, we had agreed that we would hand them over. We couldn't do that so we had to return them. That was the only thing that we could have tried. So I don't know why and how but we didn't manage to hand over the children so we returned them. This was an attempt, our attempt, to have the children transported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me try again. Who at the border refused that these children could pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably the other side. Because on the Serb side, we drove the children to the border but then the other side would not take them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must accept that then you don't know because you said "probably." Thank you so much, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go to a different topic. In addition to the Foca hospital, were there any medical schools in Foca municipality during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Certainly. In 1992, life had been disrupted in Bosnia and Herzegovina because of the war. I am one of the still-living pioneers of that project. Already on the 15th of October, 1993, we started teaching at the school of medicine and dentistry. We worked for months to organise this so that professors of Serb ethnicity who could not work in Sarajevo and who were dispersed throughout Yugoslavia, we managed to get them all back and we started out with these two faculties. They exist to this day and they have celebrated their 20th anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are -- or let me ask you this question: With respect to the professors at the school, what was the ethnic makeup of the professors at the medical faculties that you have just described which were founded in 15 October of 1993 in Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These were professors there the ranks of the Croat and Serb peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us where these professors came from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These are professors of the school of medicine from the University of Sarajevo. I used to be their student, too, and that is where I specialised. However, they left Sarajevo, and we managed to bring them to Foca and in this way to revitalize these two faculties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did the ethnic Croat professors remain at this institution for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: All the professors who came stayed at the faculty of medicine until the moment when they had to retire, when they had to retire due to their age on the basis of the Law on Higher Education.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to take a look together at 65 ter number 15257 in e-court. And the first question I will have, once the document comes up, is if you are familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, looking at the Latin description of the diagnosis, what kind of medical conditions are these -- are these people exhibiting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These are patients who were injured. They had gun-shot wounds to different parts of their body.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the name of these individuals, what comment can you make as to their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Number 7 and 8 are Carapic, so they are ethnic Serbs. And from 1 to 10, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it indicates they are being sent to the Pljevlja medical centre. Where is that located, Pljevlja?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Pljevlja is a town in Montenegro. About a hundred kilometres away from Foca. There is a hospital there that admitted these wounded persons from the medical centre in Gorazde. They probably couldn't get through, but we were 30 kilometres closer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to the next page in the Serbian and stay on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will see that the author of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the Serbian and stay on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see the author of the document is a Dr. Asim Prutina. Are you familiar with this doctor?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I know him. He's the director of the health centre in Gorazde, otherwise he is a specialist, an internal medicine specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We now -- we now see a list of individuals sent to Uzice in Serbia. Can you tell us based on the names what is the ethnic background of these patients?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you put the -- put the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put the microphones so that the interpreters can hear you and, at the same time, not so closely to your nose that breathing is the prevailing sound produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could go ahead and answer what the ethnic background of these patients.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 1, Dragoljub, is a Serb, and all the rest are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6 of the document in Serbian, page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here we have Dr. Prutina sending two patients to Sokolac. First of all, can you tell us what hospital was in Sokolac and to what entity was this hospital subordinated?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: This is the military hospital at Sokolac. It is subordinated to the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the ethnicities of the patients, can they be determined from the names?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 in Serb, page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We now have a list of individuals that were sent to the Foca hospital. First of all, looking at their names, do you have a comment as to the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These patients are of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us whether you recall such an instance in March and April of 1992 of patients being brought into the Foca hospital from Goradze to be treated?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I remember. I was one of the two surgeons in the Foca hospital. In view of their injuries that had to be treated for a longer time, I sent them to Kosevo, to the university clinical centre in Kosevo. One of them was Jusuf Preses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And looking again at the Latin, do you have a comment as to the medical diagnosis for these patients?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These are gun-shot wounds. And under number 9, Baljim Hanjalic [phoen] was not wounded. He suffered from bronchial asthma and heart problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now these patients came from the 20th of March through the 25th of April. During that entire same time-period, were you able to receive and treat wounded Serbs from Foca town itself?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: In the course of April 1992, I treated 48 patients surgically --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because of the barricade --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're being asked to please repeat the numbers. The translator did not catch them.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: In the month of April 1992, I treated 48 patients surgically. 37 of them were Muslims and the remaining 11 were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any difficulties in the time-period of March to April 1992 for wounded Serbs to travel from Foca town to Foca hospital and be treated there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: During the first eight or ten days in the month of April, we could not admit wounded males because of the barricades on the road by the penitentiary, and those patients did not dare or were not allowed to go to the hospital. The first patient I admitted was Marijan Blagojevic, who had a chest wound, and I admitted him on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you are close to 40 minutes now where the indication was 30 minutes, and you are dealing with a lot of details which either could be agreed upon or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But I tried to agree with the Prosecution but they wouldn't agree with the other list so why would they agree with this list? Your Honours, I tried to do everything in accord and now I have to ask the witness these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ethnicity, is that something you could agree on on the basis of names or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They didn't want to agree to that on the other documents, Your Honour, so I have to say that they cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you gone to the Prosecution and said: We want to use these lists and we want to establish what ethnicity they were, apart from that the statement itself says already that is no discrimination. Did you go and try to find that out -- or the wounds, what was wounded persons, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we actually did meet before this session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- and agreed to stipulate that all three of the documents that were originally being tendered contained names from the Serb ethnicity and the Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- but apart from that, even if that would not be the case, that you have used 40 minutes, could you wind up and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm done actually. So that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if you are ready, Ms. Harbour, to cross-examine the witness, you have an opportunity to start for the next six or seven minutes with that. Mr. Maric, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Harbour. Ms. Harbour is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find her to your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, Dr. Aziz Torlak was your friend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: When Serb soldiers came to the Foca hospital in April 1992 looking for Dr. Torlak, you and another doctor helped to hide Dr. Torlak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, Dr. Torlak attempted to leave Foca in an ambulance but it was stopped and he was removed and taken to KP Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Due to the threats that we all received or we saw, we suggested that Dr. Torlak should leave Foca because his life was not safe. He received documents from the authorities, and the director, Dr. Stanic, gave Dr. Torlak our ambulance. Dr. Torlak is from Rogatica. He left the hospital in that ambulance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was he then stopped and was he removed and taken to KP Dom? Because the first five or six lines of your answer are a simple "yes" to that he attempted to leave Foca. Now the rest of the question, was he -- the ambulance stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prison is 800 metres away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I visited him 15 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, could you please focus your answers on the question. Was the ambulance stopped, yes or no? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. But I'm sure that they were stopped. The ambulance was indeed stopped in front of the KP Dom because 15 days later I visited Dr. Torlak at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say: I do not know whether it stopped, whether he was removed, but I found him later in KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, I don't know. Yes, KP Dom. Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully understand that you were not present and therefore cannot say what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: But he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Really what I was interested in is the fact that he was taken to KP Dom and you've confirmed that. Are you aware that Dr. Torlak suffered a terrible death at the hands of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And I refer the Chamber to Exhibit P572, page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object that if they are going to present this kind of question to the witness, they must give the document before the witness so that the witness can comment. When they are describing a particular type of circumstances, if it's in the document and they are asking the witness to confirm, they have to show the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. If there is any dispute about it and then, of course, you can put the document to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic, but you just assisted the Chamber. The question simply was: Do you know whether Dr. Torlak met his death at the hand of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I visited Dr. Torlak 15 days later with my chief, and later I did not have any such opportunity in view of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you'd -- do you know how he died or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Dr. Amir Berberkic, another Muslim colleague of yours, he was wounded in April 1992 and you operated on him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Dr. Amir Berberkic, he was my surgical resident and I did operate on him in April. He had gun-shot wounds through both knees. Dr. Berberkic left the hospital without anybody's permission and some seven or ten days later he was admitted with all gun-shot wounds in both knees. I treated him, I operated on him, Dr. Berberkic was cured, he left the hospital, he was discharged, and I believe that he is currently in America.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: He left the hospital as a prisoner to KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: That's correct because he was later exchanged. I don't know who else was exchanged at the same time, but it is true that he was in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Harbour, when you say he left the hospital as a prisoner, was it after the operation or before the operation? I'm asking because the witness said he left without permission and I'm not quite sure which leaving you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: It was after you operated on him that he eventually left the hospital as a prisoner and was put in KP Dom; is that correct, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: He left the hospital and seven or ten days later he was admitted as a patient. I operated on him, I treated him, I cured him, and then he was taken away to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, Ms. Harbour. It's time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. But before you leave this courtroom, I want to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given already today or still to be given tomorrow, and not only not to speak to anyone but also not to communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony. If that is clear, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, the 30th of October, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
